clue.text: Strange affair of a Madagascan basket-maker

indicators.note: strange suggests the letters of the next word are in an odd, unfamiliar order

explanation.surface: An odd love affair involving a basket weaver from Madagascar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges AFFAIR. The definition is cryptically apt: the palm fibre from Madagascar is what baskets are made of.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffia is a fibre from a Madagascan palm, widely used for weaving baskets and mats.

clue.text: Seas are enveloped in 'aze, we hear, making for African port

indicators.note: enveloped in means wrapped inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: haze with its h dropped, said aloud, sounds like A's, meaning two letter As

indicators.note: we hear tells us the pieces are taken by their sound when spoken

parts.note: said aloud, seas are sounds like the letters C, C and R

explanation.surface: Seas are swallowed in a cockney haze, making for an African harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'aze signals a dropped h, so the word is said aloud like A's, the plural of the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Accra is the capital and chief seaport of Ghana in West Africa.

clue.text: Boldness with which attendant gives such important news?

parts.note: front means nerve or effrontery, boldness
a page is a young attendant, as at a wedding or court

explanation.surface: A cheeky servant passes on a big story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such' points back to the wordplay: news big enough for the paper's first sheet.
explanation.definitionFit: The most important stories in a newspaper are printed on its first sheet, so are called this.

clue.text: King taken in by a phony religious, community

indicators.note: taken in by means held inside the following pieces

parts.note: a sham is something phony or fake
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A monarch is fooled by a fraudulent sect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken in' doubles in the surface as 'fooled', a neat misdirection for the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashram is a Hindu religious retreat where a community lives under a guru.

clue.text: Condition is inserted in treaty for — non-belligerent

indicators.note: inserted in means placed within the following word

parts.note: a pact is a treaty or formal agreement
if introduces a condition

explanation.surface: A clause is added to a peace treaty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treaty' is the container, not a hint at the definition; 'non-belligerent' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who opposes war and refuses to fight is non-belligerent by conviction.

clue.text: Coaches, say, time run held by host before game

indicators.note: before puts this piece ahead of the next
held by means contained within the following word

parts.note: a publican, landlord of a pub, is a host to his customers
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
a sport is a game

explanation.surface: Sports coaches recount a race timed by a host before the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coaches' looks like sports trainers but means buses; a publican, the landlord of a British pub, is a host.
explanation.definitionFit: Coaches are an example of buses and trains open to all passengers, hence the ', say'.

clue.text: Body-builder with extra weapon

parts.note: clay is the stuff a body is made from, as Adam was formed from clay in Genesis
more means extra, additional

explanation.surface: A muscleman comes with an extra weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body-builder' is not a gym fanatic but the material bodies were made from in the Bible story.
explanation.definitionFit: A claymore is a large two-edged broadsword once used by Scottish Highlanders.

clue.text: Gang-leader has cigarette lit

parts.note: fag is British slang for a cigarette
a fire that is lit is said to be in

explanation.surface: A gang boss has his cigarette alight.
explanation.walkthrough: FAGIN is the leader of the boy pickpockets in Dickens's Oliver Twist; 'fag' is everyday British slang for a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: Fagin is the Dickens villain who runs a gang of child thieves in London.

clue.text: At last, he gets to work at Oxford, say

definitions.text: At last, he gets to work at Oxford, say

parts.words: At last, he gets to work at Oxford, say
parts.note: seems to be a man finally employed at the university, but a last is a foot-shaped block and an Oxford is a style of laced shoe

explanation.surface: A man finally finds a job in the university city.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads Oxford as the university city; in fact an Oxford is a laced shoe, and a last is the form a cobbler works on.
explanation.definitionFit: A cobbler works at a last to produce footwear such as Oxfords, so this is his trade.

clue.text: Its victims are highly alarmed

parts.note: highly alarmed seems to mean very frightened, but it means frightened when high up

explanation.surface: Sufferers from some condition are extremely frightened.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the phobia of heights, so its sufferers are alarmed when high up.

clue.text: Don't stop person making fool of himself

definitions.meaning: an urging to continue: carry on
a stupid, clownish person, a fool or oaf

explanation.definitionFit: Split in two it is the phrase urging someone to continue; as one word it is slang for a buffoon.

clue.text: Having finished with: farm animal, 1 spiced beef

parts.note: past means over, finished with, as in past caring
a ram is a male sheep on a farm
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Finished with the livestock, one turns to seasoned meat.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper prints the figure 1 as a letter-like 'I'; read as one, it gives the Roman numeral I.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastrami is seasoned smoked beef, typically served sliced in sandwiches.

clue.text: Either way, note a lot of extremely low points

indicators.note: either way says this piece reads the same forwards and backwards

parts.note: a minim is a musical note, a half note

explanation.surface: Either way you look at it, the score has many very low marks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Either way' tells you the note MINIM is a palindrome; add A.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural of the lowest value a quantity reaches, so a set of the lowest points.

clue.text: Pater's rhyme scheme

definitions.meaning: father, from the Aramaic word used in the New Testament
a quatrain whose first and last lines rhyme, as do its middle two

explanation.definitionFit: It is an Aramaic word for father and also the pattern of an envelope-rhymed quatrain.

clue.text: In part' of church, is attempt to follow bishop appropriate?

indicators.note: to follow puts these words after the bishop and appropriate pieces

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
apt means appropriate, fitting
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: Is a bishop the right person to have a go at a church area?
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link word joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The baptistry is the area of a church, or a separate building, where baptisms take place.

clue.text: Old 'road with bend before hill

indicators.note: before puts the bend piece ahead of the hill

parts.note: a turn is a bend in a road
pike is a northern English word for a peaked hill, as in Scafell Pike

explanation.surface: An old route with a curve before a rise.
explanation.walkthrough: PIKE as a hill is chiefly a Lake District usage (Scafell Pike, England's highest peak).
explanation.definitionFit: A turnpike was a road with toll gates, common in Britain before the railways.

clue.text: Religion is enshrined in quiet sacred music

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, quietly

indicators.note: enshrined in means kept inside, as a relic in a shrine

parts.note: an anthem is a piece of sacred choral music

explanation.surface: A faith is preserved in hushed church music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quiet' gives P from the musical marking piano.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantheism is a belief system holding that God and the universe are identical.

clue.text: Eternal punishment that man will dismiss

parts.note: that man will contracts to he'll
to fire someone is to dismiss them from a job

explanation.surface: He will sack you, which is eternal damnation.
explanation.walkthrough: HE'LL drops its apostrophe in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: The flames of hell are the traditional image of the everlasting torment of the damned.

clue.text: Army engineers held back by broken-down heap -—- they'll soon be gone.

indicators.note: held means kept inside, so one piece is contained
broken-down means the word heap is wrecked and rearranged
back says the engineers' letters run in reverse

parts.note: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers of the British Army

explanation.surface: Soldiers caught behind a wreck of a heap, all soon to vanish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the engineers round, and 'broken-down' rearranges HEAP to EPHA before they are held inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ephemera are short-lived things, from the Greek for lasting a day.

clue.text: Standard choice between central. characters

indicators.note: between places one piece inside the pair of others

parts.note: N and M are the two letters at the very middle of the alphabet
or is the word offering a choice

explanation.surface: A standard choice between the main characters in a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'central characters' looks like the leads of a play, but means the middle two letters of the 26-letter alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is a standard or usual pattern to which things conform.

clue.text: Comparatively quaint drinking-vessel

definitions.meaning: more odd or peculiar, comparative of rum meaning strange
a large stemmed glass or goblet

explanation.walkthrough: Rum meaning odd or peculiar is old-fashioned British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the comparative of rum (strange, in British slang) and also a large drinking glass.

clue.text: Epic Scot, good in last match

indicators.note: in means placed inside the following word

parts.note: the final is the last match of a competition

explanation.surface: A heroic Scotsman, superb in the cup final.
explanation.walkthrough: Fingal is the hero of the Ossian epics published by James Macpherson in the 1760s.
explanation.definitionFit: Fingal is the legendary Scottish hero of Macpherson's supposed Ossianic epic poem.

clue.text: Antelopes, including Eastern species grouped together

indicators.note: including means holding the next piece inside

parts.note: gnus, or wildebeest, are African antelopes

explanation.surface: A herd of antelopes contains several Asian species.
explanation.walkthrough: 'including' puts E inside GNUS, after the G.
explanation.definitionFit: A genus is the rank of classification that groups closely related species together.

clue.text: Unorthodox leader mixed up-so what!

indicators.note: mixed means the letters of the following words are jumbled together

explanation.surface: A rebellious leader is muddled and dismissive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' scrambles UP SO WHAT. A southpaw is a left-handed boxer, who leads with the right hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A left-handed boxer stands unconventionally, leading with the right rather than the left.

clue.text: Some intraverted characters to avoid

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words supplies the letters

explanation.surface: A few shy people try to dodge things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' picks letters from inside INTRAVERTED, an old spelling of introverted.
explanation.definitionFit: To avert something is to turn it aside or prevent it, which is to avoid it.

clue.text: Bridge player up against opponent of the old school

parts.note: E is East, one of the four players at bridge
to means against, as in standing face to face
N is North, an opponent of East at bridge

explanation.surface: A card player faces a rival from a traditional school.
explanation.walkthrough: At bridge North-South partner each other against East-West, so N opposes E. Eton is a famous English public school.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is the school someone attended; an old Etonian speaks of it as his old school.

clue.text: Instrument of torture first used with club

parts.note: an iron is a golf club
maiden means first, as in a maiden voyage

explanation.surface: A torture device used for the first time alongside a cudgel.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in the clue in reverse of answer order.
explanation.definitionFit: An iron maiden is a spiked, human-shaped cabinet used, by legend, to torture prisoners.

clue.text: How could nobody look after this? Right!

definitions.text: How could nobody look after this? Right!

parts.words: How could nobody look after this? Right!
parts.note: reads like an indignant complaint, but describes a parade command after which no soldier looks to the right

explanation.surface: Someone is indignant that a thing was left untended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right!' seems to be an exclamation, but it is the direction nobody looks after the drill order.
explanation.definitionFit: This military drill command makes every marching soldier turn the head the other way from right.

clue.text: Meteor exploding? Far from it

indicators.note: exploding suggests the letters are blown apart and reassembled

explanation.surface: Is a meteor exploding? Not at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exploding' rearranges METEOR; 'Far from it' looks like a denial but means distant.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote means distant, a long way away, as is anything far from a place.
